transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—I'm Dr. Smith. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, I... I didn't actually make the appointment myself. They kind of made me come in. I work down at the freight warehouse, moving materials and stock, you know, just paying the bills since I took a break from taking my college classes. But today, things got really... well, everyone got really worked up. I guess they brought me in because of what I was doing on the floor. 

See, I was working by the loading dock, right near the main forklift lane where the big pallets come through, and I just kept... freezing. Like, my body would just stop. I'd be standing right by the forklift and I'd just freeze with my arms straight up in the air, just holding them there for a long time. And the machine, it has this backup alarm, this really specific, piercing beep, and I kept copying it. I was making the exact same beeping sounds out loud, matching the rhythm perfectly, and doing all the hand signals the ground guides use, just repeating them over and over. 

And then with the freight—when I was supposed to be stacking the boxes, I wasn't just throwing them on the pallet like they want you to. I was moving them into these strange little patterns, arranging them really specifically because they just had to go in those exact spots. The foreman and the other guys were getting so mad, they were yelling at me, literally screaming over the noise of the machinery for me to stop and just load the truck the normal way, but I just kept moving them in those patterns and making the sounds. I couldn't really stop doing it even with them yelling. So... yeah, they pulled me off the floor and brought me here.

Before today, going back to when you were a child, did you always have these kinds of repetitive movements, insistence on exact patterns, or difficulty with back-and-forth social interaction, or is this something that started more recently?

No, no... I mean, when I was a kid? Not at all. I was just a regular kid, you know? I never did the freezing thing or cared about patterns back then. I used to ride my bike all over the neighborhood with my brother, and we'd build these forts out in the woods behind our subdivision. I never cared about where the branches went or if they were in some exact order, we just threw them together in a big messy pile. My mom was always yelling at me because my bedroom was a disaster, and I'd just shove all my toys and clothes under the bed to hide them. I definitely wasn't arranging anything perfectly. 

And talking to people was fine. I had friends in middle school and high school, we hung out at the mall, I went to parties... I mean, I even started college, right? I was taking business administration classes before I took this break to work at the warehouse. You don't get through all that if you can't talk to people or if you're just standing around freezing in the middle of the hallways. 

This whole thing... the patterns with the freight boxes, the freezing, the sounds... that's all just lately. It's like, recently, the air just gets really, really heavy, and my body just stops. My arms just go up on their own. I don't remember ever feeling that thickness in the air when I was little. It's like the warehouse has this specific energy now, and that forklift beep, it just gets inside my head and reverberates, and I have to let it out by making the sound back. But that never happened when I was a kid. It's just recently that the patterns started actually mattering, like the boxes *have* to go in those exact spots or everything is just wrong. But I never cared about that stuff before. So no, it's definitely not from when I was little. It's just happening now, and the foreman doesn't get it, he just thinks I'm trying to mess up the loading schedule, but I'm really not.
Have you had any recent illnesses, head injuries, or been using any drugs, alcohol, or new medications around the time these episodes started?

No, no, nothing like that. I haven't been sick, like, not even a cold or a cough or anything. I haven't been to a doctor in... well, since I got my physical for college, I think. And I definitely haven't hit my head. I wear my hard hat at the warehouse, you know, OSHA regulations and all that, the yellow one with the little ratchet strap in the back that you have to twist to get it tight enough so it doesn't fall off when you bend over to pick up the pallets. So my head is fine. 

And drugs? No. I don't do any of that. I mean, some of the guys on the loading dock, they go out to their cars on their lunch breaks and you can smell the weed on them when they come back in, especially Dave, he works the second shift, but I don't touch that stuff. It messes with your head, and I need to stay focused, especially with the forklift lanes being so narrow and the way the pallets are stacked so high. And I don't really drink either. Maybe a beer at a party back when I was taking classes, but not now. I just go to work and come home. 

And medications... no, I don't take anything. Not even Tylenol, really. I just drink water. I have this big metal water bottle I bring to work, the kind that keeps the ice from melting for like 24 hours, because it gets so hot in the warehouse, especially near the corrugated metal doors when the sun beats down on them in the afternoon. It just bakes you in there. But yeah, no pills, no sickness, no hitting my head. Just the heavy air and the freezing and the patterns. That's it.

Around the time these episodes of freezing and pattern-arranging started, have you also noticed any big changes in your mood—like feeling unusually elated, energetic, or irritable, or on the other hand, very sad, hopeless, or low on energy?

No, I... I don't think so. I mean, my mood is just my mood, you know? I haven't been bouncing off the walls or feeling super happy or anything like that. I just get up, I put on my steel-toed boots—the ones with the metatarsal guards because the safety guy, Greg, he's a real stickler about foot protection ever since that guy dropped a transmission on his foot last year—and I go to work. I don't feel energetic. If anything, the warehouse just drains you, especially with the air getting so thick like I was saying. But I wouldn't say I'm sad or hopeless either. I'm not sitting at home crying or staring at the wall feeling sorry for myself. 

I just... I just go to work, and I do what I have to do. The guys get mad at me, sure, like the foreman yelling, and maybe that's annoying, but I'm not snapping at them or getting irritable in some crazy way. I just ignore them because they don't understand about the patterns and the way the boxes have to be. They don't see it. But my mood itself? It's just flat, really. Just normal. I don't feel high, I don't feel low, I just feel... present, I guess? Just there, dealing with the heavy air and the beeping. But no big mood swings or anything like that. Just steady.
Aside from the beeping and the 'heavy air' sensation, have you been hearing voices or sounds that others don't hear, or seeing things that others don't see?

Voices? No, no, I don't hear people talking to me when there's nobody there, if that's what you mean. It's just the beeping. That loud, piercing beep from the forklift, the one that echoes off the corrugated metal walls and gets stuck right in the center of my forehead until I have to let it out. But not voices. I mean, I hear the guys on the floor talking, obviously. Like I hear Dave complaining about his back, or the foreman yelling over the intercom system—which, by the way, has this terrible static sound before he even starts talking, it's like this crackling noise that buzzes in your ears. But that's real, everybody hears that. And I don't see things either. I mean, I see the boxes, I see the patterns they have to be in, the exact alignment of the corners on the pallets, how the cardboard edges have to line up perfectly or the whole structure of the aisle feels wrong. But I'm not seeing ghosts or shadows or things that aren't there. It's just the warehouse, just the heavy air pressing down on my shoulders, making my arms go up, and the boxes, and the beeps. That's all. Nothing else. Just... just exactly what's there, but heavier, you know?

When you feel that 'heavy air' pressing down or feel the need to arrange the boxes in exact patterns, do you have a specific belief about why this is happening—like feeling it's controlled by an outside force, has special meaning, or is connected to something only you understand?

An outside force? Like... like someone with a remote control or something? No, no, nothing like that. It's not like someone is beaming thoughts into my head or making me do it. And it doesn't mean anything special, like a secret code or a message. It's not like I'm trying to spell out words with the pallets. I don't know *why* it happens, it just... it just is. Like gravity, you know? You don't ask why gravity holds the forklift on the ground, it just does. It's just the physical reality of the space. 

When the air gets heavy—and I'm telling you, it gets so thick by those loading dock doors, especially around 2:00 PM when the sun is hitting the metal siding and the dust from the cardboard is just hanging there in the humidity—the pressure just builds up. And the boxes, they just *have* to be aligned. If the corner of one of those heavy-duty double-walled boxes, the ones we use for the automotive parts that weigh like fifty pounds each, if that corner is even a quarter-inch over the edge of the wooden pallet... the whole structure of the aisle is wrong. You can feel the tension in the air. 

Gary, the foreman, he'll come stomping over with his clipboard—he always has this aluminum clipboard that clicks when he snaps the pen into it—and he'll yell, 'What are you doing, you're wasting time, wrap the pallet!' But he doesn't feel the weight of it. He doesn't understand that if I don't fix the corners, if I don't make the pattern exact, the pressure just keeps pressing down on my shoulders until my arms have to go up to hold it. But I don't have some crazy theory about it. It's not the government or spirits or anything. It's just the warehouse. It's just the way the boxes have to be so the air doesn't crush you. I don't know why nobody else notices it, but I'm just dealing with what's right in front of me. There's no secret meaning, it's just exactly what I'm telling you.
Have you noticed any other physical symptoms around this time, like fevers, muscle stiffness, tremors, seizures, or unusual changes in your heart rate or blood pressure?

Fevers? No, no fevers. I mean, it gets incredibly hot in the warehouse, obviously. Like, in mid-July, when all the loading bay doors are wide open but there's absolutely no cross-breeze coming off the asphalt parking lot, you just sweat right through your high-vis shirt. We have to wear these bright neon yellow ones, safety mandate, and they show sweat really bad right down the middle of your back. So I get hot, sure, but not sick-hot. Not a fever. 

And muscle stiffness... well, I'm lifting freight all day. Anyone would be a little stiff, right? When you're moving pallets of those automotive parts—like I was telling you, fifty pounds a box, sometimes sixty if it's the brake rotors—your lower back is going to feel it by the end of a ten-hour shift. But it's not like a weird, unnatural stiffness. It's just the job. I don't have tremors or the shakes or anything like that. My hands are completely steady. Honestly, they have to be steady to line up the corners of the boxes exactly right. If my hands were shaking even a little bit, I couldn't get the cardboard edges perfectly flush with the wood of the pallet, and then the whole pattern would be off, and the aisle would just feel completely wrong. So no, no shaking. And definitely no seizures. I've never passed out or had a seizure or anything scary like that. 

As for my heart rate or blood pressure... I mean, it's just normal for working. Sometimes when I have to hold my arms up, you know, when the air gets too heavy and thick and I have to push back against it so it doesn't just crush down on me, my heart might beat a little faster just from the physical effort of holding my arms locked in place for so long. It takes a lot of energy to hold up that kind of pressure. But it's not like my heart is just racing out of nowhere for no reason. It's just the exertion of dealing with the weight in the aisle. I actually had to do a full physical for this job—the company makes everyone go to this occupational clinic down on 4th Street before they even let you touch the forklift—and they checked all of that. My blood pressure was totally fine. Perfect, the nurse said. So physically, I'm fine. I'm not sick. It's just the environment I'm dealing with.

Have you noticed any other symptoms lately, like unexplained weight changes, joint pain, skin rashes, excessive thirst, or changes in your energy or sleep that might suggest something going on with your body overall?

Weight changes? No, I weigh exactly what I always weigh. I mean, I step on the scale in my bathroom sometimes—it's this old dial scale right next to a cracked tile near the sink—and it's always the same. 175, maybe 178 if I just ate. I eat the exact same thing every single day anyway, so there's no reason my weight would fluctuate. I pack a turkey sandwich, whole wheat bread, just a thin layer of mayo, because if you put too much on, the bread gets completely soggy by the time the 11:30 lunch whistle blows. And I always get a bag of those jalapeño kettle chips from the vending machine in the breakroom. The breakroom has this constant, buzzing fluorescent light that drives me crazy, but anyway, no, my weight is exactly the same as it was when I started the job. 

And joint pain... I mean, I told you about my lower back earlier, but that's just muscle fatigue. It's not my joints. My knees are perfectly fine. I made sure to buy these specific steel-toed boots, the heavy-duty Timberlands, and I even went to the pharmacy on Route 9 to get those extra gel arch support inserts. If you stand on solid concrete for ten hours without them, your heels feel like they're literally bruising from the inside out. But my joints themselves? They don't ache at all. They bend exactly how they're supposed to when I squat down to pick up the freight. Gary is always yelling over the intercom, 'lift with your legs, not your back,' so my knees do a lot of the work, but they don't hurt. 

Skin rashes? No, definitely not. Like I said, the high-vis shirts make you sweat a ton, and the cardboard dust is everywhere. When you rip open a new pallet of shrink wrap, this fine brown dust just poofs up and coats your forearms by the end of the shift. Sometimes that makes you itch just a tiny bit if you sweat through it, but it washes right off as soon as I get home. I use that really strong blue soap, the Irish Spring one, and it cuts right through the warehouse grime. So no, no rashes or weird spots or anything. My skin is totally normal.

As for being excessively thirsty... no, I drink a normal amount of water. It's a hot warehouse, obviously, so you have to stay hydrated. We have one of those big blue water cooler jugs over in the corner near loading bay 4, the kind you have to flip upside down into the dispenser. I'm usually the one who has to change it out because I'm the youngest guy on the floor and all the older guys act like it
Does anyone in your family—parents, siblings, or grandparents—have a history of mental illness, like schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or any other psychiatric condition?

Family history? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my family is just... normal. My dad, he manages an auto body shop out in Westlake, the one with the big faded blue sign that's been missing the 'E' for like five years now. He gets stressed out, sure, especially when the supply chain gets backed up and he's waiting on parts, like those OEM bumpers that take three weeks to ship from overseas. He'll yell and throw a wrench across the garage sometimes when he's frustrated, but that's just him blowing off steam because the customers are breathing down his neck. It's not a psychiatric condition, it's just being a mechanic, you know? 

And my mom, she's perfectly fine too. She works the morning shift at that diner over by the interstate, the one that serves breakfast all day. She's always on her feet, pouring coffee and carrying those heavy ceramic plates, so she complains about her sciatica a lot. She's actually the one who told me to get those gel inserts I bought for my work boots, because she has to wear these thick white orthopedic shoes for her shifts or her legs cramp up. But her mind? Completely sharp. She remembers the regular customers' orders before they even sit down in the booth. 

As for my grandparents... well, my dad's dad died of a massive heart attack back when I was in middle school, but that was just because he ate bacon every single morning of his life and smoked two packs of Pall Malls a day since he was sixteen. It was his heart, nothing to do with his head. And my grandma on my mom's side, she's still around, living in this little assisted living place a few towns over. She forgets where she put her reading glasses sometimes, or she'll call me by my dad's name, but she's eighty-two, so that's just what happens when you get old. It's not some big mental illness, it's just normal aging. 

And I just have one younger sister. She's eighteen, just started her freshman year at the state college. I took a few classes there myself a couple years ago before I realized sitting in a stuffy lecture hall with those awful fluorescent lights humming overhead just wasn't for me, which is why I took the freight job instead. I just needed to be doing something physical, moving things around. But anyway, my sister is doing great, she's pledging a sorority and making the dean's list and everything. So no, there's nobody in my family who has ever had to go to a psychiatrist or be put in a hospital for their brain or anything like that. We're all just regular working people. We deal with physical stuff, like my dad's bad shoulder or my mom's back, or the pressure in the warehouse for me, but that's just life. There's no history of anything else.
Since this started, have you had any blood tests, brain scans, or other medical work-ups done, and if so, did any of them show anything abnormal?

Medical work-ups? Brain scans? No, no, definitely nothing like that. Like I was telling you before, I had that one physical at the occupational clinic down on 4th Street before I got hired, where they made me pee in a cup for the drug screen and checked my blood pressure and everything, but that was months ago, way before any of this started. Since the air in the warehouse started getting so heavy and the pressure started pushing down on me in the aisles, I haven't been to any doctors or hospitals or clinics. 

I mean, why would I need a brain scan? My brain is completely fine. It's the environment that's the problem, the actual physical weight of the space I'm having to hold up. A blood test isn't going to show anything about that. 

Besides, I really don't have the time to go sit in some freezing cold waiting room reading five-year-old car magazines. I work ten-hour shifts, Monday through Thursday, and by the time Friday rolls around, I'm just totally exhausted from physically pushing back against the atmosphere all week. And I hate needles anyway. When they did my bloodwork for that college physical a couple years ago—back when I was taking those classes I told you about—the nurse tied that rubber tourniquet so tight it pinched the skin right on my bicep, and she still had to dig around with the needle to find the vein. My veins are actually really easy to see now, you know, because of all the heavy lifting, the vascularity you get from moving the freight, but I still don't want anyone poking me. 

And those brain scans, like MRIs? I saw a documentary about those once when I was up late. They slide you into this tiny, claustrophobic tube that sounds like a literal jackhammer right next to your ears for forty-five minutes. I couldn't do that. I already have to deal with feeling crushed and trapped in the aisles at work, I'm not going to go to a hospital and let them shove me in a tube to do it to me on my day off. So no, no blood tests, no scans, nothing abnormal on any medical charts because I haven't had any tests done. I haven't needed to. I'm just trying to manage the situation at the warehouse.
Can you tell me exactly when this all started—was it something that came on suddenly within the last day or two, or has it been building up gradually over several weeks or months?

Suddenly? No, no, it wasn't like I just woke up yesterday and everything was suddenly like this. It's been way longer than a few weeks, too. It’s been building up for a while... I mean, things have really been going downhill for about eleven months now. 

Yeah, eleven months, because I know exactly when it started. It was right after I moved. I was trying to make my commute easier, you know? I was still taking a couple of those classes at the state college back then, before I dropped them, and I was working at the warehouse, so I was driving back and forth across town all day in my old Honda Civic. The transmission slips in third gear, so sitting in stop-and-go traffic on I-95 was just a complete nightmare every single afternoon. So I found this shared apartment. It’s right in the middle, much closer to work and school. I figured, perfect, I'll save on gas, I won't have to deal with the highway as much, it made total sense on paper.

But that’s exactly when it all started. Right after I moved in with these two other guys—one of them is a line cook who works nights, and the other just plays video games all day, I swear he never even leaves the couch—anyway, I moved my stuff in, which wasn't much, just my mattress, a dresser, and some boxes. And almost as soon as I got settled in that new place, about eleven months ago, that’s when I first started noticing the atmosphere changing. 

It was gradual at first. Like, I’d be walking down the hallway of the apartment building—it has this awful peeling yellow wallpaper and always smells like stale cigarettes and boiled cabbage—and I'd just feel this slight... resistance in the air. Like the air was just a little thicker, a little heavier than it used to be. And then it just kept getting worse, building up and building up over the months, following me from the apartment all the way to the warehouse, until the pressure got to where it is now, where I have to physically brace myself and push back against it just to walk down the freight aisles. So yeah, definitely not a sudden thing. It's been a slow, downhill slide for eleven solid months.
Have you noticed any other new physical symptoms during this same period, such as unexplained neurological changes—like weakness, numbness, difficulty walking, or vision changes?

Weakness? Numbness? No, no, nothing like that. I mean, think about it... if I was weak or had trouble walking, there is just no way I'd be able to keep my job at the warehouse. I'm on my feet on solid concrete for ten hours a day, walking miles and miles back and forth across that floor. I actually track my steps on my phone sometimes, and it's crazy how much ground I cover. So my legs work perfectly fine, even if my knees get a little sore, which is why I got those gel inserts I mentioned. 

And I'm definitely not weak. I'm lifting forty, fifty-pound boxes of industrial supplies and heavy machinery parts all shift. If anything, I'm a lot stronger now than I was back when I was just sitting at a desk at the state college. I *have* to be strong, you know, just to physically push back against that heavy air I was telling you about. It takes a lot of muscle just to stand upright and keep moving forward when the atmosphere is pressing down on you like a literal weight. 

And numbness... no, I feel everything. Probably too much, honestly. When I scrape my knuckles against the metal shelving in aisle four—which happens way more often than it should because the aisles are too narrow and they stack the pallets way too close together—I definitely feel it. I feel the rough cardboard on the boxes, the freezing cold metal handle of the pallet jack... no numbness at all anywhere on my body. 

And my vision is completely fine, too. 20/20. It has to be, because I'm constantly having to read these tiny little faded barcodes and SKUs on the shipping labels. Half the time I'm doing it over by the loading dock where the lighting is just terrible because management hasn't bothered to replace the overhead bulbs that burned out like three months ago. If my eyes were going bad, I'd be loading the wrong pallets onto the wrong freight trucks, and my supervisor, Gary—he's this guy who always wears these really loud plaid shirts and complains about his alimony payments—he would be all over me. But he never has to correct my pulls, because I can see everything perfectly. 

So, no, no neurological stuff, no weakness, no vision problems. My physical body is totally normal. It's just the environment I'm having to fight against.

During these episodes of freezing or feeling the heavy air, do you ever become confused about where you are, what day it is, or have trouble staying oriented, or is your mind clear and aware the whole time?

Confused? No, no, I'm never confused. My mind is completely clear the entire time. Honestly, it's probably clearer than anyone else's in that building because I'm the only one actually paying attention to what's happening with the atmosphere. 

I know exactly where I am and what day it is. I have to. Like I said, I work ten-hour shifts, Monday through Thursday, and we have strict quotas. If it's a Wednesday at 2:15 PM, I know exactly that I'm standing in aisle seven—that's the one with all the heavy industrial adhesives that always smell faintly like vinegar—and I know I need to get my pallet to the staging area before the 3:00 PM outbound truck pulls into bay four. I wear this cheap black Casio watch, the resin kind, and I check it constantly, so I never lose track of time. 

When the freezing happens, when the air just turns to solid lead and pins me down, it’s not because I’m lost in my head or forgetting where I am. It's the exact opposite. I am hyper-aware. I’m standing there, physically unable to push forward, but mentally? Mentally I’m taking in everything. I can see the dust motes just hanging there, suspended in the thick air because the pressure is keeping them from falling. I can hear Gary yelling at someone over by the loading dock, or the forklift backing up on the other side of the warehouse—that loud beep, beep, beep echoing off the corrugated metal roof. I know exactly where the exits are, I can see the red LED exit sign flickering down by the breakroom. 

I know my name, I know I'm twenty years old, I know I dropped my classes at the state college, I know I live in that awful apartment with the peeling yellow wallpaper, and I know exactly what I'm doing. My mind is racing, really, trying to calculate the physics of how to break through the density of the space in front of me so I can just take one single step. So, no, there's no confusion at all. I'm completely oriented. I'm entirely present. It’s just that the physical space around me solidifies, and I'm trapped inside it while being totally, one-hundred-percent awake and aware of every single second that ticks by.

Over these past eleven months, have you noticed yourself pulling away from friends or family, losing interest in things you used to enjoy, or just feeling less motivated to do things outside of work, even before the freezing and pattern behaviors started?

Pulling away? No, no, it’s not like that. I haven't been isolating myself or anything, if that's what you mean. I mean, I still talk to my mom every single Sunday. She calls me right after she gets back from church, usually around 11:30 AM, and we talk for at least an hour. She always asks if I'm eating enough, which is funny because I'm burning so many calories at the warehouse I have to eat constantly just to keep my weight up. 

And as for friends... well, I never really had a massive group of friends to begin with, you know? I've always been a pretty independent guy. Back at the state college, before I dropped my classes—which, by the way, I didn't drop because I lost interest, I dropped them because the schedule was just impossible with the warehouse shifts and that awful commute on I-95 that I was telling you about. But even back then, I mostly just kept to myself. I'd go to class, sit in the back, take my notes, and leave. I wasn't in any fraternities or clubs or anything. 

So it's not like my social life took some huge nosedive. I still talk to the guys I live with, too, when they're actually around and awake. The line cook, he's usually asleep during the day, but sometimes we'll cross paths in the kitchen and talk about the baseball scores or whatever while he's making his coffee before his shift. And the other guy, the one who plays video games 24/7, sometimes I'll grab a soda and just sit on the couch with him for an hour and watch him play that new open-world RPG that just came out. I still really enjoy watching him play, even if I don't play it myself because my hands are just too cramped up from gripping the pallet jack all day at work.
